proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel credits Marx with prompting his philosophical self-education and later retains dialectical analysis while rejecting reductive class formulas.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 first answer recalls evening philosophy courses to understand Capital, followed by disenchantment rather than permanent doctrinal allegiance. Own 2019 dialectic answer explicitly says this approach reconciled him with Marx while adding sociological understanding of state and culture. No full Marx original newly read; his empirical reconstruction and mixed intellectual resources remain distinct.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel acknowledges Althusser’s injunction to learn theoretical thinking as an exercise that later helped him challenge philosophical pretension.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 first answer says he retained intellectual gymnastics after Marxist disenchantment and used them against pseudo-treatises of historical epistemology. This is a bounded methodological resource, not endorsement of all Althusser’s philosophy or proof of direct personal teaching. No exact original Althusser work is identified or read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel names reading Foucault among the formative philosophical work through which he learned to defend his historical research practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 formation account says an initially alienating theory course incited intensive reading of Lévi-Strauss, Althusser, Foucault, Deleuze and Lacan, through which he gradually forged intellectual tools. Foucault is one of several credited authors, not a sole teacher or wholesale allegiance. No specific title, direct supervision or original body reading is invented; the broader collective reading is retained explicitly.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly credits Elias’s work as an important resource in developing his sociohistorical research.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2019 socio-historian answer says he relied extensively on Elias and regards him as one of the founders of socio-history. This is Noiriel’s retrospective acknowledgment and terminology, not an atlas claim that one scholar founded the whole field. It coexists with Noiriel’s more restrictive 2006 distinction reported by Hamman; neither complete original book is newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel uses Weber to distinguish practical historical inquiry from foundational epistemology and to analyze power relations as capable of solidarity as well as domination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 answers invoke Weber’s anatomy/walking analogy and the practical language needed to defend research, explicitly unable to recall the exact latter text. Own 2019 explains his relational conception with Weber and uses legitimate violence in discussing state formation. These are attributed conceptual uses, not exact Weber quotations independently authenticated or acceptance of every historical generalization.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Veyne’s historical epistemology for addressing professional historians in language he regards as accessible mainly to philosophers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 first answer specifies Comment on écrit l’histoire and objects to the gap between the professed historian audience and philosophical language. The criticism concerns practical disciplinary usefulness and asymmetries of authority, not a rejection of every Veyne argument. He also acknowledges the broader reflexive evolution associated with Veyne and de Certeau. Veyne’s book and replies are not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Furet’s denunciation of positivism for blurring the authority of journalistic intervention and scholarly historical research.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2012 Bouveresse answer names Furet and argues that attacks on positivism could undermine research autonomy by putting a Nouvel Observateur article on the same plane as a scholarly article. This is Noiriel’s retrospective critical judgment, with his own allowance for multiple legitimate activities when clearly characterized. No particular Furet article, original exchange or reply newly read; no blanket assessment of Furet’s scholarship.

proposed_edges.relationship: Noiriel opposes the position he attributes to Latour that social science is only a form of literature, using Bouveresse’s defense of science as a resource.

proposed_edges.relationship: De Vries credits Brewer’s material culture and consumption seminar invitation with reactivating his household research and leading to his first Western industrious revolution articles.

The claim is a concrete scholarly stimulus, beyond mere attendance, not sole origin, coauthorship of all subsequent work or adoption of every cultural history position. proposed_edges.relationship: De Vries explicitly describes Wrigley’s work as a scholarly standard he has striven to attain throughout his career.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2008 preface xi ties Wrigley’s 2000 McArthur lecture invitation to this explicit acknowledgment, then credits the wider learned and critical Cambridge audience for clarifying how to turn the lectures into the book. This supports an acknowledged intellectual model, not formal supervision or attribution of the entire household theory to Wrigley. The reverse Wrigley use of de Vries and van der Woude, edge2623, is a separate empirical appropriation.

proposed_edges.relationship: De Vries challenges the sufficiency of an imposed work discipline account associated with Thompson when explaining increased early modern labor, stressing household consumption incentives while retaining exploitation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1994 page258 places Thompson’s specific work discipline quotation within a criticism of portraying workers as initially nonacquisitive and in need of training as both workers and consumers. Note26 cites Time, Work, Discipline,90, visually checked in the actual article. The adjacent Pollard quotation is a separate co-target. De Vries then contrasts literary and historical evidence of material aspirations, but page260 explicitly recognizes self-exploitation of wives and children, lost leisure and other social harms. This records his bounded disagreement, not proof that Thompson denied every consumer motive or that increased labor was universally free or beneficial. Original Thompson essay and historical witnesses remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: De Vries criticizes Stearns’s definition of consumerism for its conceptual shortcomings while also directing readers to Stearns’s historiographical overview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2008 page5 note13 calls Stearns’s Consumerism in World History definition remarkable chiefly for its shortcomings. He separately criticizes Steven Miles’s distinction between consumption and consumerism and insists on distinguishing acquisition from final consumption and allowing multiple dimensions of utility. The note ends with Stearns’s 1997 periodization overview as a reading reference. This is a particular definitional criticism, not rejection of all Stearns scholarship; Miles’s argument and the broader critique are not silently assigned solely to Stearns. Neither original Stearns nor Miles text newly read.
